$comment: Provenance for the lesser GraphQL schema contentus validates its documents against.
WHY A PINNED COPY AND NOT INTROSPECTION. A client that asks the instance what its
schema is can only ever discover that it agreed with whatever it was pointed at.
The question this repository needs answered at BUILD time is different: do the
documents contentus sends match the contract lesser publishes? That contract is a
file in the lesser repository at a known ref, so it is pinned here by digest and
the answer is deterministic, offline, and identical on every machine.
TWO CHECKS, AND THEY ANSWER DIFFERENT QUESTIONS.
`sha256`, `bytes` and `git_blob_sha1` are checked OFFLINE by
`scripts/audit-graphql-contract.mjs` on every build. They establish that the bytes
in the tree are unchanged since someone wrote these values down. That is all they
establish. Every one of them lives in this repository and moves in the same commit
as the schema, so an author who fabricates an SDL and updates all three produces a
tree that is perfectly self-consistent and still wrong — and a `ref` of forty `f`
characters is invisible to an offline check, because nothing offline dereferences
a ref. Adversarial review demonstrated both. Offline integrity must therefore
never be reported as provenance.
`repository`, `ref` and `upstream_path` are checked ONLINE, by
`scripts/verify-schema-provenance.mjs` in `.github/workflows/schema-provenance.yml`.
It dereferences the git object at <repository>@<ref>:<upstream_path> and compares
it with the bytes here. The binding is git's own content addressing: a blob OID is
a pure function of the bytes, so the OID computed locally is directly comparable
with the OID GitHub reports, with no local value trusted in between. A fabricated
schema moves the OID; a wrong repo/ref/path does not resolve; a stale schema meets
a different object. None of those can be repaired by editing another field here,
which is what makes it a binding rather than a restatement.
MOVING THE PIN. Copy the file from lesser at the new ref, update `ref`, `sha256`,
`bytes` and `git_blob_sha1` together, run `pnpm run validate:graphql` for the
documents and `node scripts/verify-schema-provenance.mjs` for the upstream object.
Every document is re-validated against the new schema, so a field lesser removed
fails the build in the same commit that adopts the removal — which is the entire
point of pinning it rather than trusting it. `git_blob_sha1` is exactly
`git hash-object <file>`.
This file is READ BY A GATE. `gov-infra/verifiers/strict-json.mjs` semantics apply:
a duplicate key is a value the reviewer reads and a different value the control
enforces, so duplicates are rejected rather than last-wins.
The canonical schema is one self-contained SDL document: `type Query` plus the
`extend type Query` blocks that carry the CMS, messaging, agent and drone
surfaces. graphql-js merges extensions when building, so the CMS fields
contentus reads (`articles`, `articleBySlug`, `draftPreview`, `myDrafts`,
`sharedDraftReviews`) resolve from the same build as the core schema.
Where the gate looks for documents. `src` is walked whole — every TypeScript
module AND every Svelte component, because a component's <script> can declare
and send a document exactly as a module can, and a walk keyed on `.ts` would
have been a file-set assumption dressed up as coverage.
Where execution starts. The vendored-tree boundary asks whether contentus can
EXECUTE a document-bearing vendored module, and execution begins at the two
build entries — the same two `vite.config.ts` names as rollup inputs. A module
no entry reaches cannot run, whatever else imports it.
WHY THIS IS NAMED RATHER THAN 'every file outside the tree'. That earlier
formulation treated an ORPHAN as a root. `src/lib/lesserTimelineStore.svelte.ts`
is vendored source the greater CLI drops at the lib root; nothing in this
repository imports it, and it pulls in the whole `greater/adapters` barrel. Under
a correct resolver the old formulation is unsatisfiable for a reason that has
nothing to do with what contentus runs. It only ever passed because the previous
resolver could not follow `./LesserGraphQLAdapter.js` to a `.ts` file.
The narrowing is not a weakening, and it is not taken on trust:
tests/graphql-contract.test.mjs runs the REAL two-pass Vite build and asserts
that every module either pass loads is inside this closure, and that no declared
vendored document module is loaded by either. The gate also prints how many
outside files reach a forbidden module without being executable, so the
narrowing is counted rather than silent.
Vendored greater-components source, managed by the `greater` CLI and never
hand-edited. Its adapter layer carries GraphQL documents written against
GREATER's own projection of a fediverse server — `Account`, `Post`, `Status` —
and lesser's schema has no such types at all (`type Account` does not exist;
the equivalent is `type Actor`). Validating them against lesser's contract
does not report a contract defect, it reports that they answer a different
contract.
THIS IS A DISCLOSURE, NOT A PERMISSION. The counts below are asserted exactly:
a vendored document appearing, disappearing, or changing shape fails the gate
and has to be re-declared deliberately. And the reason the exclusion is SAFE is
checked rather than asserted — `boundary` below is the control, and
tests/graphql-contract.test.mjs re-proves it against the real build, where a
module that is loaded is a module that can execute.
upstream_trees.reason: greater-components adapter documents target greater's own schema (Account/Post/Status), which lesser does not define; contentus does not import or execute them
upstream_trees.boundary: no module outside this tree may reach a document-bearing module inside it
